cards.front: The net reproductive rate, R0, is the sum over ages of {{c1::l_x m_x}}: the chance a newborn female is alive at age x times the average daughters per live female at that age.
cards.back: R0 = sum of l_x m_x, counted per generation, not per year.
cards.quote: Whether a population can replace itself depends on the net reproductive rate, R0

cards.front: In a closed population with fixed rates, what does R0 above 1 or below 1 mean for successive generations?
cards.back: Above 1, each generation is larger than the last; below 1, each is smaller. R0 = 1 means exact replacement.
cards.quote: Above 1, each generation is larger than the last; below 1, smaller.

cards.front: Why is a population projection from R0 a prediction rather than an observation?
cards.back: It assumes a closed population with rates that stay fixed, but real vital rates change with density, weather and year.
cards.quote: It is a prediction from assumptions, not an observation: real vital rates change with density, weather and year.

cards.front: In a cohort life table, survivorship is l_x = {{c1::n_x / n_0}}, the fraction of the original cohort alive at exact age x.
cards.quote: is the number alive at exact age x, l_x = n_x / n_0
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: In a life table, m_x is the expected (average) number of {{c1::daughters per live female}} at age x.
cards.back: Tables of this kind usually count females only.
cards.quote: the average number of daughters per live female at that age

cards.front: In a life table, d_x is {{c1::the number that die between age x and age x + 1}}, calculated as n_x minus n_(x+1).
cards.back: Summed over all ages, d_x accounts for every member of the cohort.
cards.quote: how many die between age x and age x + 1?
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: Why is the age-specific death probability q_x calculated as d_x / n_x rather than d_x / n_0?
cards.back: Only the animals alive at the start of the interval are at risk of dying in it. Dividing by the original cohort gives d_x/n_0, not q_x.
cards.quote: Only the 40 alive at age 2 were at risk.
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: A closed cohort of 250 newborn females has n_1 = 150, n_2 = 60 and n_3 = 15. Find l_2, d_1 and q_1.
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: In a life table, what does the symbol q stand for, and what is it easily confused with?
cards.back: q_x is a death probability for an age interval. It is not the allele frequency q of population genetics.
cards.quote: This q is a death probability, not the allele frequency q of population genetics.
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: The probability of surviving an age interval is p_x = {{c1::1 − q_x}}.
cards.quote: Whatever does not die survives: p_x = 1 − q_x
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: Why is survivorship l_x a product of the interval survival probabilities p_x before age x?
cards.back: Reaching age x means surviving every earlier interval in turn, each conditional on the one before, so the product rule of probability applies (l_3 = p_0 × p_1 × p_2).
cards.quote: That is the product rule from probability and crosses, each stage conditional on the one before
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: A cohort has interval survival probabilities p_0 = 0.9, p_1 = 0.6 and p_2 = 0.5. What is l_3?
cards.quote: Reaching age 3 means surviving year 0, then year 1, then year 2, so l_x is a product of the p_x before it
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: A worked cohort has l_x m_x = 0, 0.8, 0.8 and 0.1 at ages 0 to 3 years. What is R0?
cards.back: R0 = 0 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.1 = 1.7 daughters per newborn female.
cards.quote: From the table: 0 + 0.8 + 0.8 + 0.1 = 1.7 daughters per newborn female.
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: An invented closed cohort of female voles has l_x = 1.0, 0.6, 0.25 and m_x = 0, 1, 2 daughters per female at exact ages 0, 1 and 2 months; none survive past 2 months. Find R0 and say whether the population grows with fixed rates.
cards.back: R0 = 1.0 × 0 + 0.6 × 1 + 0.25 × 2 = 1.1 daughters per newborn female. Above 1, so it grows each generation.
cards.quote: at each age, the chance a newborn female is alive (l_x) times the average number of daughters per live female at that age (m_x), added over her life

cards.front: The cohort generation time, T, is {{c1::the mean age of mothers when their daughters are born}}.
cards.back: T = sum of x l_x m_x / R0.
cards.quote: The cohort generation time, T, is the mean age of mothers when their daughters are born.
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: A cohort has x l_x m_x = 0.8, 1.6 and 0.3 at ages 1, 2 and 3 years, and R0 = 1.7. What is the generation time T?
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: A cohort produces equal numbers of daughters at ages 1 and 2 years. Females now also start producing some daughters at age 3. Does the generation time T rise, fall or stay at 1.5 years?
cards.back: It rises above 1.5 years. T is a weighted mean age of mothers at birth, so births at an older age pull the mean up.
cards.quote: Ages 1 and 2 alone would average 1.5; the few daughters born at age 3 pull the mean up.
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: How does the shortcut r ≈ ln(R0)/T turn a per-generation multiplier into a yearly rate?
cards.back: ln(R0) is the continuous growth rate per generation; dividing by the generation time T gives a rate per year.
cards.quote: ln(1.7) is the growth rate per generation, and dividing by T gives a rate per year.
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: Why is r ≈ ln(R0)/T only an approximation of the intrinsic rate of increase?
cards.back: It treats T as the length of every generation, but births are spread over several ages.
cards.why: The exact r solves the Euler-Lotka equation.
cards.quote: Births spread over several ages make this an approximation.
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: The yearly multiplier is {{c1::lambda = e^r}}; with r = 0.334 per year, it is about 1.40, roughly 40% more each year.
cards.quote: The yearly multiplier is lambda = e^r = e^(0.334), about 1.40: roughly 40% more each year.
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: A vole cohort has R0 = 1.1 and generation time T = 1.45 months. Estimate r with the shortcut, and the monthly multiplier lambda.
cards.back: r ≈ ln(1.1)/1.45 = 0.0953/1.45 ≈ 0.066 per month. lambda = e^0.066 ≈ 1.07, about 7% more each month.
cards.quote: A common shortcut treats T as the length of every generation
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: Two populations both have R0 = 1.7. One has T = 1.59 years, the other twice that. Predict the sign and relative size of r for each.
cards.back: Both r are positive because R0 is above 1. With the shortcut, r is about 0.334 per year for the first and about half that, 0.167, for the second.
cards.why: R0 sets the sign of r; T only changes how fast growth happens.
cards.quote: R0 above 1 gives a positive r and R0 below 1 a negative one; T only changes how fast.
cards.section: Generation time and a yearly rate

cards.front: Why does a Type II survivorship curve plot as a straight line on a logarithmic axis?
cards.back: Type II is a constant probability of death per interval, so l_x = (1 − q)^x and log l_x = x × log(1 − q): the same step down each year.
cards.why: It is a constant probability, not a constant number of deaths.
cards.quote: log l_x = x × log(1 − q), a straight line falling by the same step each year
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: A cohort of 640 shows Type II survivorship with a yearly death probability of 0.5. How many die during the third year of life (ages 2 to 3)?
cards.back: 80. Survivors fall 640, 320, 160, so half of the 160 alive at age 2 die. Deaths shrink as the cohort shrinks.
cards.quote: In symbols, a constant q gives l_x = (1 − q)^x
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: A cohort's death probabilities rise with age: q_x = 0.20, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00. Which survivorship type does it sit nearest?
cards.back: Type I. Rising death probability with age means survival is relatively good early and losses concentrate late.
cards.quote: the worked cohort, with q_x rising, sits nearer Type I
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: In an invented population, 20% of newborns die within days of birth and the rest all live to exactly 60. What is life expectancy at birth, and does anyone die at that age?
cards.back: 0.2 × about 0 + 0.8 × 60 = about 48 years. No one dies at 48; heavy infant mortality drags the mean down.
cards.quote: Life expectancy at birth is the mean length of life over all newborns, so heavy infant mortality drags it far down.
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: How does an age-structure diagram (age pyramid) differ from a survivorship curve?
cards.back: A pyramid shows the proportion of the population in each age class now, which depends on past births as well as survival. A survivorship curve follows survival with age.
cards.quote: it shows the proportion of a population in each age class now, which depends on past births as well as survival
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: An age pyramid has a broad base. A student concludes the species has Type III survivorship. Evaluate.
cards.back: Not supported. A broad base may reflect a growing population with good juvenile survival, since each year's newborns outnumber the last.
cards.quote: A pyramid with a broad base is not a Type III curve; it may be a growing population with good juvenile survival.
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: With fixed rates and no migration, a population converges toward a {{c1::stable age distribution}}: the shares in each age class stop changing while the total grows or shrinks.
cards.back: The shares depend on both survival and the growth rate.
cards.quote: a population converges toward a stable age distribution: the shares in each age class stop changing while the total grows or shrinks
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: A population with many young people drops its fertility to replacement today. Why does it keep growing for decades?
cards.back: The number of women of reproductive age is still rising as the large young cohorts grow up. This is demographic momentum.
cards.quote: It can keep growing for decades, because the number of women of reproductive age is still rising as the large young cohorts grow up.
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: Why does the replacement figure of about 2.1 children per woman not apply everywhere?
cards.back: It holds only where few children die before adulthood. Where child mortality is high, more births per woman are needed to replace each generation.
cards.quote: The often quoted replacement figure of about 2.1 children per woman applies only where few children die before adulthood.
cards.section: Survivorship curves and age structure

cards.front: What are the strength and the main drawback of cohort follow-up for building a life table?
cards.back: It gives l_x and m_x directly, but slowly: for a long-lived species, one cohort can outlive a research career.
cards.quote: It gives l_x and m_x directly, but slowly
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: A static life table treats animals of different ages, born in different years, as one cohort. What population condition makes that simplest to justify?
cards.back: A stationary population: about the same number born each year and the same age-specific death rates for many years. Every age must also be sampled fairly.
cards.quote: The simplest case where that is fair is a stationary population
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: A static life table is built from carcasses found in the field. Predict the likely bias in estimated juvenile survival, and why.
cards.back: Juvenile survival is overestimated: young remains are fragile and easily missed, so early deaths are undercounted.
cards.quote: Young remains are fragile and easily missed, so a carcass table can undercount early deaths
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: How can mark-recapture data separate detection probability from survival?
cards.back: An animal seen after a gap was alive and missed. Across many animals, sightings and gaps let a model estimate detection separately from survival.
cards.why: After the last sighting, the model usually cannot tell death, permanent departure or a miss apart.
cards.quote: An animal seen after a gap was alive and missed
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: An animal still alive when a study ends is {{c1::right-censored}}: counted at risk while seen, never as a death.
cards.quote: An animal still alive when the study ends, or lost to an accident in a study of natural deaths, is right-censored
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: In a survival study, sick and weak animals are more likely to be lost from observation and are recorded as censored. Predict the effect on estimated survival.
cards.back: Survival is biased upward. Censoring is fair only if it is unrelated to the risk of dying; here the censored animals were the ones most likely to die.
cards.quote: animals lost because they were sick or weak bias survival upward
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: Name two data problems that blur life-table estimates without necessarily biasing them, and what each hides.
cards.back: Few old individuals: small samples hide gradual changes in mortality, so old ages are least certain. Pooled years: average rates hide good and bad years.
cards.quote: Small samples at old ages hide gradual changes in mortality
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: Apparent survival is true survival multiplied by {{c1::site fidelity}}, the chance a surviving animal stays in the study area.
cards.back: So permanent emigration pulls apparent survival below true survival.
cards.quote: apparent survival is true survival multiplied by site fidelity
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: Of banded adult birds, 54% are seen at the colony the next year. Detection is 0.9 and site fidelity 0.75 (invented values). Estimate true annual survival and mortality.
cards.back: True survival ≈ 0.54 / (0.9 × 0.75) = 0.54 / 0.675 = 0.80, so annual mortality is about 20%, not 46%.
cards.why: The return rate is lowered by missed birds and emigrants as well as deaths.
cards.quote: If detection is 0.9 and fidelity 0.8, an apparent return of 0.60 would point to true survival near 0.6/(0.9 x 0.8), about 0.83
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Only 60 of 100 banded adult birds are seen at their colony the next year. Design a study that separates death from the other reasons a bird goes unseen.
cards.back: Search repeatedly over seasons and years and fit a Cormack-Jolly-Seber model (detection); search neighbouring colonies or track birds (emigration); double-mark some birds (band loss); record unseen birds as unknown fates, not dead.
cards.quote: lowered by three things besides death: birds alive at the colony but not seen, birds alive that moved elsewhere for good, and birds that lost their bands
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A Cormack-Jolly-Seber model on banded gulls estimates apparent survival of 0.70. Later searches of neighbouring colonies find banded birds long missing from the home colony. What does this show?
cards.back: Some 'lost' birds had emigrated, not died, so true survival exceeds the apparent 0.70. Apparent survival includes site fidelity.
cards.quote: a survivor that left looks like a death
cards.section: Where the numbers come from, and what they miss

cards.front: With fixed rates, the exact intrinsic rate r solves the {{c1::Euler-Lotka}} equation.
cards.back: For the worked table, exact r = 0.347 per year versus 0.334 from the shortcut.
cards.quote: With fixed rates, the exact r solves the Euler-Lotka equation
cards.section: The exact yearly rate

cards.front: The shortcut r ≈ ln(R0)/T is approximate. Is the conclusion 'R0 above 1 means growth' also approximate?
cards.back: No. Scaling every m_x moves lambda across 1 exactly where R0 crosses 1, so the sign rule is exact; only the size of r is approximate.
cards.quote: so the sign rule in the one idea holds exactly; only the size of r is approximate
cards.section: The exact yearly rate

cards.front: In a cohort with R0 = 1.7, first-year survival is permanently halved while all later p_x and all m_x stay the same. Predict R0 and the population's fate.
cards.back: Every later l_x halves, so every l_x m_x halves and R0 = 0.85. Below 1, the population declines.
cards.why: l_x is a product of earlier p_x, and R0 is the sum of l_x m_x.
cards.quote: Reaching age 3 means surviving year 0, then year 1, then year 2, so l_x is a product of the p_x before it
cards.section: The worked cohort, column by column

cards.front: A static life table is built by counting living animals at each age in a growing population and reading the counts as one cohort's survivors, with no correction. Predict the bias in survival at older ages.
cards.back: Older age classes look smaller than a cohort would, because they were born when the population was smaller, so survival to older ages is understated.
cards.why: Static tables assume stationarity; growth must be corrected for.
cards.quote: its older age classes were born when the population was smaller
cards.section: Static tables when a population grows
